title: Food for the bereaved
hook: make food for the family of Ja'far, for what has come to them (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday, three days: Umm Habibah's perfume, and grief given real time, with a door out. Today, a pot on the stove.

A casserole dish with masking tape on the bottom and a name in marker. A tray of rice left on a doorstep. A neighbor who doesn't knock, just texts: it's outside. Some grieving households end up with a kitchen full of other people's cooking. In Islam, that habit has a sentence behind it, and a name: Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin. When news of his death reached Madinah, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, didn't give a speech. He gave an instruction about dinner.
screen: `A DISH WITH A NAME ON THE BOTTOM.` → `NEWS OF JA'FAR.` → `AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT DINNER.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, told by Ja'far's son 'Abdullah. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: make food for the family of Ja'far, for something has come to them that keeps them busy. Look at the reason. Not that they're sad, though they were. That they're occupied. A death takes over a household: the washing, the shroud, the prayer, the burial, the visitors, the phone calls, the children who need explaining to. Nobody in that house is thinking about lunch, and somebody has to. So the instruction lands on the neighbors, not the family. Jurists later drew a quiet lesson from the same hadith: the burden runs one way. The neighbors cook for the bereaved household, and the household isn't put to the work and expense of feeding a crowd. Now look back over the week. Gentle words at the deathbed. The body washed with care. Everyone in the same white shroud. The community standing in prayer. The grave, facing the qiblah. Three days with a door out. And now a pot of food carried across the street. Much of it is done with hands and feet rather than speeches: washing, wrapping, standing, digging, cooking. In these texts, much of the way through a death is a list of tasks, done for someone who can't do them right now.
screen: `MAKE FOOD FOR JA'FAR'S FAMILY.` · `THEY ARE OCCUPIED.` · `THE NEIGHBORS COOK.` · `A WEEK OF THINGS DONE BY HAND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a household you know that is carrying a loss, this month or this year, and think what they might actually eat: something simple, something that keeps. Picture the dish on their doorstep, left without needing thanks. If no one comes to mind, let one of the week's words stay with you: soft words, careful hands, white cloth, standing, earth, three days, food.
Food for the bereaved. The Prophet's instruction to cook for a grieving family, because what has come to them keeps them busy. Today's word.
Your line: feed the grieving. A pot of rice, left on a step. That's the week, done.

howItsDone: Muslim neighbors and relatives bring meals to a bereaved household in the first days after a death, following the hadith in Abu Dawud about the family of Ja'far, so the family doesn't have to cook or host.

chat.says: A Muslim coworker just lost her dad. Is there anything useful I can do?
options: Bring food. The Prophet said to cook for a grieving family, since loss keeps them busy.
Wait until her three days pass; helping before then isn't allowed for outsiders.
Send nothing; the hadith says only relatives may cook in a house of mourning.
chat.meaning: The Prophet said: make food for the family of Ja'far, for something has come to them that keeps them busy. The neighbors cook; the grieving are fed.

Ja'far.meaning: the Prophet's cousin, whose family was fed after his death

Madinah.meaning: the city where the Prophet lived and led the community

Abu Dawud.meaning: compiler of the Sunan, a major hadith collection

qiblah.meaning: the direction Muslims face in prayer, toward the Ka'bah

notes: Editor: removed the unsourced claim that cooking was the Prophet's first response ('he started with dinner', 'first instruction'); the week look-back no longer says every practice is done by hand (deathbed words and the standing prayer are not); ended on a concrete image instead of uplift.

The jurists' point (the family should not bear the cost of feeding guests) is stated generally; some cite a report of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah in Ibn Majah. Confirm phrasing.
